before: Whichever age it picks on, saving everybody was never your job. At fifteen you probably didn't even have your own money, or anywhere else to go. And actually, not to beat a dead horse here, but every age of you was stuck with whatever it had then, even the adult you were last year. Hindsight being 20/20 doesn't change that. You still did what you did, though, and if it hurt people or damaged a life, that may need repair.
after: (Not written yet. The next paragraph, from the guide: "Big fuckity whoopty doo, what are you gonna do for me?" is still a literal question; the first answer may be that the love stays even when it isn't believed; then trust can update from evidence. Don't say any of that here.)
brief:
- the guide: "Instead of asking which version deserves blame, ask:" In the article's words: instead of asking which age of you deserves the blame, ask these.
- the guide's six questions, in plain words: What was that age of you trying to get, or get away from? What did it understand back then? What options could it actually see, and stand to take? What happened because of the choice? What was missing: what ability, help, or protection? What can you learn, repair, or do differently now?
- A short list is fine here: the article has numbered lists elsewhere. Keep each question short, in the article's voice, and don't explain them or add a line after them that sums them up.
- The paragraph before ends on what you actually did maybe needing repair; the last question picks that up, so don't say it again.
- Say "that age of you" or "that younger you", never "the kid" or "that version".
length: a lead-in sentence and the six questions, 50 to 90 words
guide_passage: Instead of asking which version deserves blame, ask: What was that version trying to accomplish or avoid? What did they understand at the time? What options could they actually see and tolerate? What happened because of the choice? What capacity, support, or protection was missing? What can the present adult learn, repair, or do differently now?
next: “Big fuckity whoopty doo—what are you gonna do for me?” is still a literal question. But the first answer may be relational rather than practical: the love remains even when it is not believed. Trust can then update from both relational and ordinary-life evidence—being heard without retaliation, admitting where a complaint is true, repairing after an internal attack, keeping a boundary, attending an appointment, or handling one neglected problem.
